en: Now, when building
workflows, no matter if you're using AI or
not, and therefore also when you're building
AI agents,
it's likely that not all
steps need to run one after another, or
maybe not all steps should run one after
another.
And thus far in this course, that's
essentially the only case we had, right? We
ran all our steps in sequence, sequential,
which means one step after another. And we
did that because many of our steps did
depend on each other. And if step B depends
on step A,
it of course needs to run after step A.
The last workflow I showed you where we
generated a blog post with an image was a
perfect example for that. We ran all these
steps in sequence and there's nothing wrong
with that. For many workflows, that's
exactly what you need, like for this
workflow. But there also are workflows where
you can run tasks or steps in parallel,
which means side by side at the same time
essentially.
And you would do that or you could do that
if steps don't depend on each other. And
it's especially useful if steps maybe take a
bit longer because if you have step A
and that step takes quite some time and step
B doesn't depend on it,
Well, then it might make sense to run steps
A and B in parallel so that step B doesn't
have to wait for step A to finish just to
get started.
And I'll show you an example for that in
just a second.
You can also run steps conditionally, which
means you
would have 2 steps, for example, that depend
on each other. So step B may depend on the
result of step A
and Step B therefore will run conditionally
depending on what the result of step A was,
and it may be skipped depending on that
result. And I'll show you an example for
that as well in just a second.
And you can also repeat steps, so run them
multiple times.
That might make sense if you wanna refine a
result over time, if you gather feedback, or
if you're building a chat application where
you want to allow the user to ask follow-up
questions.
But actually, I'll show you examples for all
4 categories in the next lecture.
